title: B-R-K
hookLine: bracha (blessing), berech (knee), breichah (pool): blessing bends and flows

cards: Evening, outside a town, at a well. A servant has walked a long way with ten camels, sent to find a wife for his master's son.
Before he asks anything of anyone, he brings the camels down onto their knees beside the water.
In Hebrew, the verb for making them kneel is built on bet, resh, kaf, the same three letters as baruch, the first word of a blessing. Only then does the servant pray.
The root of blessing, down in the dust beside the water.

teach.b: B-R-K. Four ways in. First, bracha: a blessing.
Baruch, blessed, from three days ago, grows from these letters.
Second, berech: a knee. In Psalm 95, the call to worship says "let us kneel before the LORD," and the Hebrew for kneel is from this root.
In the Amidah, the standing prayer, a custom traced to the Talmud has people bend the knees at baruch, bow at atah, and stand straight again for God's name. The body says the word.

Third, breichah: a pool, water gathered low where the ground bends down to hold it. Dictionaries list the knee and the blessing under the same letters. Whether they began as one word is a question for linguists.
But some readers hear them together: blessing is something you bend toward, and something that pools and flows.
Fourth, the week behind you. It began with dots, the nikud that give letters a voice. Then your first word, shalom.
Then the Shema's first two words, a silent eye and a dot that moved. Then baruch atah. Then shoresh, the root under the word, and the first root, sh-l-m, peace as wholeness.
And now b-r-k, the root under the blessing you learned to read. A week ago these were single letters. Now they're words you can sound out, and roots you can dig up.

how: In the Amidah, worshippers bend the knees at the word baruch, bow at atah, and straighten before God's name; the Hebrew words for blessing and knee are listed under the same three letters, b-r-k.

games.q: the Amidah begins, and you reach the words baruch atah, then God's name. what does the custom do with the body?
o: bend the knees, bow, then stand straight for the Name.
games.why: bend at baruch, bow at atah, and straighten for the Name. the body says the word.

practice: If you're able, stand; sitting is fine too.

Bring to mind one thing from this week you're grateful for, small and real, and slowly let your knees bend a little, the way the custom bends at baruch, then straighten, or if you're seated, bow your head and lift it.
Once is enough; then sit and let the thanks pool, and if you pray, you can say baruch atah as you bend.

wordCard.voice: B-R-K. Bet, resh, kaf: the root of bracha, blessing, sitting beside berech, knee, and breichah, pool. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a blessing, from the root bet, resh, kaf.

carryVoice: Your line: blessing bends. Thanks can gather low, like water. That's a week of reading.
